title: How a purchase works
summary: The steps from agreeing a price to holding registered title to a home or land in Grenada.
body:
Buying property in Grenada follows a well-worn path, and knowing the order of events makes it far less stressful. Most purchases take somewhere between two and six months, with the longer end usually explained by an Alien Landholding Licence for buyers who are not Grenadian.

It starts with an offer. If you are buying through an estate agent, the agent normally puts your offer in writing, and once the seller accepts, both sides confirm it in an acceptance letter that goes to each party's lawyer. From this point you need your own attorney-at-law; the seller's lawyer acts for the seller, not for you.

The seller's lawyer then prepares a sale agreement, which your lawyer reviews before you sign. On signing, the buyer usually pays a deposit of around 10 per cent of the price, held by a lawyer until completion. Read the agreement's terms on the deposit carefully: it should say when it is refundable, for example if title turns out to be defective or a non-citizen buyer's licence is refused.

While the agreement is in place, your lawyer searches the title to confirm the seller owns what they are selling, free of mortgages, claims or restrictions that would affect you. A survey may be needed to confirm the boundaries. If you are not a citizen, the Alien Landholding Licence application runs in parallel.

When everything is clear, the conveyance is prepared and signed, you pay the balance through your lawyer, and the seller's lawyer releases the deed. The final step is registration of the conveyance at the Deeds and Land Registry, which is what makes your ownership a matter of public record. Your lawyer will also pay the stamp duty that falls on you, and the seller pays the property transfer tax, which the law does not allow to be passed on to the buyer.

sources.title: The buying process in Grenada (Century 21 Grenada)
Buying property in Grenada: legal guide (Forrester Law Chambers)
Aliens (Land-Holding Regulation) Act: registration in the Deeds and Land Registry

title: Title searches and surveys
summary: How to check that the seller owns what they are selling, and that the boundaries are where you think.
body:
A title search is the single most important protection you have when buying land or a house, and it is your lawyer's job, not the seller's. The search traces the chain of deeds recorded at the Deeds and Land Registry to confirm that the person selling actually owns the property, and to reveal anything registered against it, such as a mortgage that must be paid off at completion, a right of way across the land, or a dispute.

Family land deserves particular care. Much land in Grenada has passed down through generations without a formal transfer at each death, so the person offering to sell may be one of several heirs. In that case the title may need to be put in order, sometimes through probate or letters of administration, before a sale can safely go ahead. A good lawyer will tell you plainly if that is the position.

A survey confirms what is on the ground. A licensed land surveyor measures the boundaries, checks them against the survey plans on record and identifies any encroachments, such as a neighbour's wall or a building that strays over the line. For bare land, especially if it is being cut from a larger parcel, a new survey plan is usually needed before the land can be conveyed. Published guides put surveyors' fees at around 0.5 per cent of the land's value, though it varies with the size and difficulty of the plot.

If you are buying a house, consider a separate building inspection by an engineer or experienced contractor. Roofs, foundations, drainage and the quality of any additions matter a great deal in a hurricane zone, and an inspection costs little compared with the repairs it can reveal.

sources.title: Due diligence when buying property in Grenada (Forrester Law Chambers)
Buying guide: surveyor's fees and process (Terra Caribbean Grenada)

title: Buying as a non-citizen
summary: The Alien Landholding Licence: who needs one, what it costs and how to apply.
body:
Anyone who is not a citizen of Grenada, and any company under foreign control, needs an Alien Landholding Licence to own land in Grenada. The requirement comes from the Aliens (Land-Holding Regulation) Act, and the Ministry of Finance directs applicants to the Prime Minister's Office, which grants the licences. A licence only takes effect once it has been registered at the Deeds and Land Registry, and only after all the fees and duties have been paid.

The licence fee is the cost that most surprises overseas buyers: published guides consistently put it at 10 per cent of the property's value, payable on top of the purchase price. There is also a small stamp duty on the licence itself, a registration fee, and your lawyer's charges for preparing the application. On a EC$1,000,000 house, the licence fee alone would therefore be around EC$100,000, so build it into your budget from the start.

Applications are made through a Grenadian lawyer. Applicants are typically asked for a police record, character references and a banker's reference, alongside details of the property. Processing usually takes a few months and runs alongside the rest of the conveyancing, which is why purchases by non-citizens take longer. Make sure your sale agreement says the deposit is refundable if the licence is refused.

People who acquire Grenadian citizenship through the Citizenship by Investment programme by buying approved real estate are exempt from the licence requirement for that investment. Grenadians living abroad who have kept their citizenship do not need a licence at all, so check your status, and that of any spouse buying jointly, with your lawyer before you apply for one you may not need.

sources.title: Property tax and Alien Landholding Licence (Ministry of Finance, Grenada)
Aliens (Land-Holding Regulation) Act
Buying FAQ: licence fee and documents required (Century 21 Grenada)
Alien Land Holding Licence process (Forrester Law Chambers)

title: Mortgages and finance
summary: Borrowing to buy or build in Grenada, and what local lenders look for.
body:
Most mortgages for property in Grenada come from local commercial banks and credit unions. Overseas lenders rarely lend against Caribbean property, so even buyers who live abroad usually end up borrowing locally or paying cash.

Lenders look at three things: your ability to repay, the property, and your deposit. Expect to show proof of income, often several months of bank statements and a letter from your employer or, if you are self-employed, accounts and tax returns. The property must have good title, so the lender's own lawyer will usually review the title search, and the lender will ask for an independent valuation. You will need buildings insurance in place, and many lenders also ask for life cover so the loan is repaid if something happens to you. Deposits vary by lender and by borrower; published guidance suggests some local lenders accept deposits as low as 10 per cent for residents, while non-residents are commonly asked for more.

Credit unions are often worth approaching first if you are a member. They tend to know their members well, and can be more flexible about irregular income, which matters for the self-employed and for people returning home whose earnings history is overseas.

If you plan to build rather than buy, most lenders release a construction loan in stages as the work progresses, inspecting the site before each payment. They will want approved building plans, a realistic budget and, often, quotes from your contractor before they agree.

Remember the costs on top of the loan. Stamp duty is charged on the mortgage deed as well as on the conveyance, and the lender's legal and valuation fees are normally passed to the borrower. Ask each lender for a full list of charges so you can compare offers properly.

sources.title: Buying guide: financing your purchase (Terra Caribbean Grenada)
Costs on a purchase, including stamp duty on the mortgage (Forrester Law Chambers)

title: Taxes and transfer costs
summary: Stamp duty, property transfer tax, the licence fee for non-citizens and annual property tax in Grenada.
body:
It helps to separate the one-off costs of buying and selling from the tax you pay every year as an owner.

On a purchase, the buyer pays stamp duty on the conveyance, generally quoted at about 1 per cent of the price, plus their own lawyer's fees, which published guides put at around 2 per cent of the price with VAT at 15 per cent charged on the fee. A non-citizen buyer also pays the Alien Landholding Licence fee, published at 10 per cent of the property's value.

The seller pays the property transfer tax, set by the Property Transfer Tax Act. The rate depends on whether the seller is a citizen: guides published by agents and lawyers give 5 per cent for citizens of Grenada and members of the OECS, and 15 per cent for non-citizens. Under the Act, the tax is charged only on the value above EC$20,000. It is the seller's liability, and a Grenadian law firm notes that it is unlawful to shift it to the buyer, so be wary of any agreement that tries. The seller also usually pays the estate agent's commission, typically quoted at 5 per cent plus VAT.

Once you own the property, you pay annual property tax to the Inland Revenue Division under the Property Tax Act. It is charged on the assessed market value, with separate rates for land and buildings and for each class of property, such as residential, commercial and agricultural. Published examples range from nothing for agricultural land to 0.5 per cent of value for commercial land. Grenada does not charge capital gains tax on a sale.

Because these figures are set by law and occasionally change, ask your lawyer for a written estimate of every cost before you sign the sale agreement.

sources.title: Property tax and Property Transfer Tax Act (Ministry of Finance, Grenada)
Taxes and fees for buyers and sellers (Century 21 Grenada)
Who pays what on a property transfer (Forrester Law Chambers)
Grenada buying costs (Global Property Guide)

title: Building on land you own
summary: Planning permission from the Planning and Development Authority, and how to manage a build in Grenada.
body:
Owning land does not on its own give you the right to build on it. Under the Physical Planning and Development Control Act of 2002, the development of land in Grenada requires the written permission of the Planning and Development Authority, which is supported by the Physical Planning Unit. That covers new houses, extensions, changes of use and the subdivision of land. If the Authority refuses an application, the Act provides for an appeal to the Physical Planning Appeal Tribunal.

An application is normally prepared by an architect, draughtsperson or engineer and includes site plans and building drawings, with details of access, drainage and how sewage will be handled. The Authority checks the proposal against the physical plan and the building standards, and may ask for changes. Build in time for this; starting work without approval risks an order to stop or even to remove what has been built, and lenders will not release construction loans without approved plans.

Choose your contractor carefully. Ask to see buildings they have completed, speak to their past clients, and get at least two detailed written quotes that list materials and labour separately. A written contract should set out the price, a payment schedule tied to stages of completed work rather than dates, the timetable, and who is responsible for defects. Avoid paying large sums in advance.

Grenada lies within the hurricane belt, and building to the code pays for itself. Roof fixings, reinforcement in columns and beams, and window protection are where corners are most often cut, and where an independent engineer's inspection at key stages is most valuable, especially if you are overseeing the build from abroad.

sources.title: Physical Planning and Development Control Act No. 25 of 2002 (UNEP LEAP summary)
Land Development (Control) Act 1968: planning permission

title: How a purchase works
summary: The steps from an agreed price to a registered deed of conveyance in St Vincent and the Grenadines.
body:
A property purchase in St Vincent and the Grenadines follows a sequence that will feel familiar to anyone who has bought in the United Kingdom, and it runs through lawyers on both sides.

Once you and the seller agree a price, usually with an estate agent's help, the seller's lawyer prepares a sale agreement that your own lawyer reviews before you sign. On signing, the buyer normally pays a deposit of around 10 per cent, which takes the property off the market and is held by a lawyer until completion. The agreement should say when that deposit is refundable, particularly if you are a non-citizen and need an Alien Land Holding Licence that might be refused.

Your lawyer then examines the title, producing what is known as an abstract of title: the history of the deeds recorded at the Registry, showing that the seller owns the property and what, if anything, is registered against it. Non-citizen buyers apply for their licence at the same time.

At completion, the seller signs a deed of conveyance prepared by the lawyers, you pay the balance of the price, and the deed is stamped and registered. Registration is what makes you the owner of record. Stamp duty must be paid before the deed is registered, and the Inland Revenue Department will not stamp a deed of sale while property tax on the land is in arrears, so a tax check on the seller's account is part of the process.

Purchases in Mustique and Canouan, where much of the land sits within private estates, can work differently, with additional consents and rules set by the estate company. Ask your lawyer to explain the position before you sign anything there.

sources.title: Buying property in St Vincent and the Grenadines: step by step (Chestertons)
St Vincent and the Grenadines buying guide (Global Property Guide)
Stamp duty and property tax clearance on transfers (Expanship)

title: Title searches and surveys
summary: Checking ownership, family land and boundaries before you buy in St Vincent and the Grenadines.
body:
Before you hand over the balance of the price, your lawyer should be satisfied that the seller has good title. The search runs back through the deeds recorded at the Registry to show how the property came to the seller and whether anything, such as a mortgage, a lease or a right of way, is registered against it. The result, the abstract of title, is worth reading with your lawyer rather than simply filing away.

Family land is common in St Vincent and the Grenadines, and it is where most title problems arise. Land often passes through several generations without a fresh deed being recorded, so the person selling may share it with other heirs who also need to agree, or may need to obtain probate or letters of administration first. A sale that skips this step can leave the buyer exposed to claims years later.

A survey confirms that the land on the ground matches the land on paper. A licensed land surveyor fixes the boundaries, compares them with the plans on record at the Lands and Surveys Department, and flags any encroachment. If you are buying part of a larger parcel, it will need to be surveyed and subdivided first, and subdivision of land requires planning approval in its own right.

For a house, add an independent structural inspection. In a country exposed to hurricanes and, around La Soufrière, to volcanic risk, the condition of the roof, the reinforcement in the structure and the drainage around the building all deserve a professional eye before you commit.

sources.title: Abstract of title and the conveyancing process (Global Property Guide)
Due diligence and inspections when buying in SVG (Horizon Realty)

title: Buying as a non-citizen
summary: Who counts as an alien under the law, how the Alien Land Holding Licence works and how its fee is calculated.
body:
Under the Aliens (Land-Holding Regulation) Act, land in St Vincent and the Grenadines may not be held by an "unlicensed alien", and land held without a licence can be forfeited to the Crown. Non-citizens, and companies under foreign control, therefore need an Alien Land Holding Licence before ownership can pass to them. The licence is granted by the Governor-General, applies only to the land it describes, and has no effect until it is registered at the Registry of Deeds.

Not everyone who lacks a Vincentian passport is an alien under the Act. A Commonwealth citizen who is domiciled in the country and has lived there for at least seven years is treated as belonging to St Vincent and the Grenadines, as is anyone who is or has been married to a citizen. Nationals of several OECS and nearby territories, including Grenada, Saint Lucia and Dominica, are also treated as non-aliens where their country offers the same right in return, subject to obtaining security clearance from the minister responsible for national security.

The licence fee is set by a schedule in the Act according to the value of the property. As published, a purchase worth up to EC$100,000 attracts a fee of EC$10,000; between EC$100,000 and EC$3,000,000 the fee is EC$10,000 plus 6 per cent of the value above EC$100,000; and above EC$3,000,000 it is EC$184,000 plus 4 per cent of the excess. On a EC$1,000,000 home, that works out at EC$64,000. Schedules can be amended, so ask your lawyer to confirm the current fee.

Applications are made through a local lawyer, with personal details, a police record and information about the property, and typically take a few months. Make the sale agreement conditional on the licence being granted.

sources.title: Aliens (Land-Holding Regulation) Act, Chapter 316, with Schedule of fees
Alien Land Holding Licence in practice (Chestertons)

title: Mortgages and finance
summary: Borrowing to buy or build in St Vincent and the Grenadines, and preparing a strong application.
body:
Mortgages for property in St Vincent and the Grenadines come mainly from the local commercial banks and the credit unions. Lenders outside the region seldom lend against property here, so buyers living abroad usually borrow locally or buy with cash.

A lender will want to see that you can afford the repayments, that the property is good security, and that you have a deposit. Prepare proof of income, such as recent payslips and bank statements, or accounts and tax returns if you work for yourself. The lender will instruct its own valuation and will rely on your lawyer's title report, so title problems on family land can stop a mortgage as surely as a sale. Buildings insurance is a condition of almost every mortgage, and many lenders require life cover as well.

Credit unions are an important source of housing finance here and are often more flexible with members whose income is irregular. If you are a member, or can become one, it is worth asking them early.

For self-build, lenders generally release money in stages as the work is inspected, so you will need approved building plans, a costed budget and quotes from your contractor before the first payment. Keep the receipts for everything; it makes each drawdown quicker.

Non-citizens should expect to be asked for a larger deposit, and may find that some lenders will only consider the application once the Alien Land Holding Licence has been granted. Whatever your circumstances, ask each lender for a complete list of fees, covering valuation, legal costs and the stamp duty charged on the mortgage deed, and compare the total cost rather than the interest rate alone.

sources.title: Financing, deposits and costs when buying in SVG (Chestertons)
Aliens (Land-Holding Regulation) Act: licences to hold mortgages

title: Taxes and transfer costs
summary: Stamp duty on the deed, the Alien Land Holding Licence fee, legal fees and property tax in SVG.
body:
The main government charge on a property sale in St Vincent and the Grenadines is stamp duty on the deed of conveyance, which must be paid before the deed can be registered. Published guidance most often describes it as 10 per cent of the price shared equally, with the buyer and the seller each paying 5 per cent, though some sources refer to lower rates on lower-value property. Because the basis is not consistently described, ask your lawyer or the Inland Revenue Department to confirm the exact charge for your purchase before you sign.

On top of stamp duty, the buyer pays a registration fee, generally quoted at between 0.25 and 1 per cent, and their own lawyer's fees. A non-citizen buyer also pays the Alien Land Holding Licence fee, which is set by the schedule in the Aliens (Land-Holding Regulation) Act according to the property's value: EC$10,000 for property up to EC$100,000, then EC$10,000 plus 6 per cent of the value above EC$100,000, up to EC$3,000,000. Sellers usually pay the estate agent's commission, commonly around 5 per cent.

As an owner, you will pay annual property tax to the Inland Revenue Department. Keep it up to date: the Department will not stamp a deed of sale or a mortgage while property tax is in arrears, so unpaid tax can hold up both your own future sale and any borrowing against the property.

Add these costs together before you agree a price. For a non-citizen buying a EC$1,000,000 home, the licence fee of about EC$64,000 and a 5 per cent share of stamp duty alone come to over EC$110,000, before legal fees. A written estimate from your lawyer at the outset avoids unpleasant surprises at completion.

sources.title: Stamp duty on property transfers in SVG (Expanship)
Aliens (Land-Holding Regulation) Act: Schedule of licence fees
Buying costs in SVG (Chestertons)
SVG buying costs (Global Property Guide)

title: Building on land you own
summary: Planning approval from the Physical Planning and Development Board, inspections and choosing a builder.
body:
New buildings, extensions and changes of use in St Vincent and the Grenadines need the approval of the Physical Planning and Development Board, with applications handled by the Physical Planning Unit. Notices of applications for commercial and other significant developments are published in the Government Gazette, giving the public a chance to see the plans and object in writing, so larger projects should allow for that period.

Applications are prepared by an architect, draughtsperson or engineer and include detailed plans showing the location and design of the building. The Physical Planning Unit reviews the technical detail and puts the application to the Board, which approves or refuses it. The building regulations introduced in the mid-2000s brought staged inspections during construction, covering the setting out, the foundations before concrete is poured, the structural frame and roof, the reinforcement of ring beams, the plumbing and drains and the electrical work, ending in a final inspection before a certificate of occupancy is issued. Plan your build around these inspections; skipping them can cause problems with insurance, lending and any future sale.

Take care choosing a contractor. Visit buildings they have finished, ask previous clients about quality and timekeeping, and get detailed written quotes. Your contract should fix the price, link payments to completed stages of work rather than to calendar dates, and say who is responsible for putting right defects.

St Vincent and the Grenadines faces hurricanes and, near La Soufrière, volcanic hazards. Building properly to the code, with sound roof fixings, reinforced concrete work and good drainage, protects both your family and your investment.

sources.title: Physical Planning and Development Board applications (Government Gazette, March 2024)
Building regulations: plans, approval and staged inspections (Searchlight)

title: Returning-national programmes
summary: Grenada's Welcome Home Programme: who qualifies, what it covers and how to apply.
body:
Grenada's main support for people coming home is the Returning Nationals Programme, officially called the Welcome Home Programme. It is a package of tax concessions for Grenadian nationals who have lived abroad and are returning to live in Grenada permanently.

To qualify, you must be a Grenadian national who has lived abroad continuously for at least seven years and has decided to return for good. You will be asked for proof: a one-way ticket to Grenada, evidence of your years overseas, and a packing list of everything you are shipping or plan to ship.

The programme offers a full exemption from duty and tax on household and personal effects, new or used, up to a value of EC$75,000, and a 50 per cent concession on one personal vehicle per family. You can bring the vehicle with you or buy it locally. The Ministry of Finance's notices have also listed tax incentives for returning nationals who set up a business.

Applications are handled by the Returning Nationals Facilitation Bureau, the concession desk at the Ministry of Finance, which you can call on +1 473 440 2731 to make an appointment. Customs and Immigration no longer process these applications. Timing matters: claims must be made within three months before or after your return, so contact the Bureau while you are still planning the move rather than after your container lands.

The concessions come with conditions, the most important being that goods and vehicles cannot be sold within three years without repaying the duty and tax that was waived. The details of what you ship and the vehicle are covered in the next articles in this guide.

sources.title: Returning Nationals Programme (Ministry of Finance, Grenada)
Changes to the Returning Nationals Programme (Ministry of Finance, Grenada)
Concession procedures for returning nationals (Consulate General of Grenada)

title: Planning the move
summary: A practical timeline for moving home to Grenada, built around the concession deadlines.
body:
The best moves home are planned backwards from the date you intend to arrive, because the Returning Nationals Programme has firm time windows. Claims for concessions must be made within three months before or after your return, and shipped goods should ideally arrive no more than three months before you do.

Six to twelve months ahead is the time to gather paperwork while you still have easy access to it overseas: evidence of your seven years abroad, such as tax returns, payslips, tenancy agreements and bank statements; your children's school records and immunisation history; your medical records and prescriptions; and, if you are bringing a vehicle, its registration and purchase documents. Make sure every family member's Grenadian passport or birth certificate is in order.

Three to six months ahead, decide what is worth shipping. The household and personal effects allowance is generous at EC$75,000, but freight is not cheap, and some appliances are better bought locally where spares and service are available. Get quotes from shipping companies and choose a customs broker in Grenada to clear your goods. Prepare a detailed packing list as you pack; Customs will want it.

In the final month, contact the Returning Nationals Facilitation Bureau at the Ministry of Finance to book your appointment, arrange somewhere to stay while you settle, and keep originals of every document in your hand luggage rather than in the container.

Once you arrive, work through registrations in a sensible order: your TIN with the Inland Revenue Division, National Insurance if you will work, a bank account, a local driver's licence, and school places for children. The articles in this guide cover each one.

sources.title: Returning Nationals Programme (Ministry of Finance, Grenada)
Concession procedures for returning nationals (Consulate General of Grenada)

title: Shipping and customs
summary: Shipping your household goods to Grenada and clearing them under the returning nationals allowance.
body:
Under the Returning Nationals Programme, qualifying Grenadians can import household and personal effects free of the Common External Tariff, VAT and the Customs Service Charge, whether the items are new or used, up to a total value of EC$75,000.

Your goods can be shipped ahead of you, but they should ideally arrive no more than three months before your permanent return. The application for the concession needs a packing list of everything you have shipped or will ship, so make one as you pack, room by room, with a realistic value for each item. Keep receipts for anything new.

Most people use a customs broker in Grenada to clear a container or crate. The broker prepares the customs entry, liaises with the Ministry of Finance's concession desk and Customs, and arranges delivery once the goods are released. Agree the broker's fee in advance and give them copies of your concession approval as soon as you have it.

Two conditions catch people out. Items you import duty-free are for your own use, and if you sell them within three years of importing them you will have to pay the duty and tax that was waived. And anything above the EC$75,000 allowance, or anything that does not count as household and personal effects, such as goods for a business, will be charged at the normal rates.

If you are not a returning national, published guidance from a Grenadian estate agency suggests that duties on personal and household goods for non-nationals are around 45 per cent, though the actual charge varies by item. Get a broker's estimate before you ship.

sources.title: Returning Nationals Programme (Ministry of Finance, Grenada)
Concession procedures for returning nationals (Consulate General of Grenada)
Relocating to Grenada (Terra Caribbean)

title: Bringing a vehicle
summary: The 50 per cent vehicle concession for returning nationals, the environmental levy and the conditions on resale.
body:
Returning nationals who qualify for the Welcome Home Programme are entitled to a 50 per cent concession on one personal vehicle per family. You can ship a vehicle from the country you have been living in or, if you prefer, buy one in Grenada and claim the concession there.

If you import a vehicle, it must come from the country where you lived continuously for the seven years before your return. Age matters in two ways. The procedures published for returning nationals say the vehicle must be five years old or less to qualify for relief, and the environmental levy, which is charged separately, depends on the vehicle's age: the Ministry of Finance gives 2 per cent of the cost, insurance and freight value for vehicles of one to five years old, and 30 per cent for vehicles over five years. A consulate's version of the procedures applies the 2 per cent rate to vehicles up to four years old, so check the current rule with the Ministry's concession desk before you buy or ship.

The concession comes with a three-year condition. If you sell the vehicle within three years of the concession being granted, you must repay the taxes that were forgone. Some import guidance also notes that if you leave Grenada for an extended period, Customs expects to be told, and duties may become due.

Grenada drives on the left, and right-hand-drive vehicles, including used Japanese imports, are common and accepted. Before shipping, compare the total cost of freight, the levy and your share of the duty with the price of a similar vehicle bought locally with the concession; for many people, buying locally works out simpler.

Changes to the Returning Nationals Programme (Ministry of Finance, Grenada)

title: Housing
summary: Renting first, buying or building: finding somewhere to live when you return to Grenada.
body:
Many returning Grenadians find it wise to rent for the first few months, even if they plan to buy or build. It gives you time to get to know different areas again, to see how long the commute really takes on Grenada's winding roads, and to look at property without the pressure of a deadline.

Rentals are advertised through estate agents, online and, very often, by word of mouth. Most homes on the island are stand-alone houses rather than apartments. Before you sign a lease, check who pays for water and electricity, whether there is a water tank for when the supply is interrupted, and how the property has fared in past storms. Ask for a written tenancy agreement that sets out the rent, the deposit and the notice period.

If you are buying, our Property and investment guide explains the process step by step, including title searches, the costs of a purchase and the annual property tax. Grenadian citizens do not need the Alien Landholding Licence that non-citizens pay for, but a spouse who is not a citizen may be affected if you buy jointly, so raise it with your lawyer early.

If you already own family land and plan to build, you will need planning permission from the Planning and Development Authority before work begins, and you should make sure the land is properly in your name first. Family land that has never been formally transferred is one of the commonest causes of delay for returning nationals, and it is best sorted out by a lawyer before you spend money on plans.

Water is supplied by the National Water and Sewerage Authority, NAWASA, and setting up accounts for utilities usually requires identification and, for tenants, a copy of the lease.

sources.title: Relocating to Grenada: housing and utilities (Terra Caribbean)
Grenada buying guide (Terra Caribbean)

title: Banking
summary: Opening a bank account in Grenada, the Eastern Caribbean dollar and moving money home.
body:
Grenada uses the Eastern Caribbean dollar, issued by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank and shared with seven other countries and territories in the region. It has been fixed to the US dollar at EC$2.70 to US$1 for decades, which makes planning your finances from abroad easier, at least for US dollar income.

Grenada has commercial banks, including Republic Bank Grenada and the Grenada Co-operative Bank, and a strong network of credit unions. Many returning nationals keep an account with each: a bank for international transfers and a credit union for savings and, later, loans.

Opening an account is straightforward but paperwork-heavy, because banks must confirm who you are and where your money comes from. Expect to provide your passport, proof of your address in Grenada (a utility bill or tenancy agreement), your Taxpayer Identification Number, and often a reference letter from your current bank overseas. If you are moving savings or the proceeds of selling a home abroad, bring evidence of where the money came from, such as a sale completion statement; banks will ask, and having it ready avoids delays. Holders of US citizenship or green cards will also be asked for US tax information under international reporting rules.

Open your account soon after arriving, or even before you move if your bank allows it, because you will need it for utility deposits, a car purchase and receiving any pension. When transferring large sums, compare the exchange rate and fees offered by your bank abroad, your Grenadian bank and specialist transfer services; the difference on a house deposit can be substantial.

If you will receive a pension from abroad, ask the paying authority about payments to an account in Grenada, and keep your overseas account open until the first payments arrive safely.

sources.title: The Eastern Caribbean dollar peg (Global Property Guide)
National Insurance Scheme Grenada: banks

title: Healthcare
summary: Public hospitals and health centres, private care and health insurance in Grenada.
body:
Grenada's public health service is run by the Ministry of Health. Primary care is delivered through health centres and medical stations across the island's health districts, where basic care is free or low-cost for residents. The main referral hospital is the General Hospital in St George's, supported by Princess Alice Hospital in St Andrew's, Princess Royal Hospital on Carriacou and the Mt Gay psychiatric hospital.

Alongside the public system is a sizeable private sector of hospitals, clinics and specialists, mostly in and around St George's. Many residents use both: public health centres for routine care and private doctors when they want a quicker appointment or a particular specialist. Private care is usually paid for at the time of treatment.

There is no national health insurance scheme in Grenada, although one has been discussed for years. Private health insurance is available from regional insurers, including Sagicor and Guardian, and from international insurers. Returning nationals over 50 should look at this carefully before they leave their current country, because cover is easier and cheaper to arrange before any new condition is diagnosed. Check whether a policy covers medical evacuation to a larger hospital overseas, which matters for serious illness or injury.

Before you move, gather your medical records, a summary from your current doctor, and a supply of any regular medication with the prescriptions, as some brands may not be available. Register with a doctor or your local health centre soon after you arrive so that you are known before you need urgent care.

Some specialist treatment is not available on the island, so serious conditions may involve travel to Trinidad, Barbados or further afield. Factor that into both your insurance and your savings.

sources.title: Grenada's public and private healthcare (Pacific Prime)
Healthcare in Grenada (Immigrant Invest)

title: Schools
summary: Enrolling children in Grenada's schools and transferring their records from abroad.
body:
Grenada's school system follows the familiar Caribbean pattern. Primary education is compulsory from about age five to twelve, followed by secondary school from around twelve to seventeen, ending with the Caribbean Secondary Education Certificate examinations set by the Caribbean Examinations Council. Teaching is in English, and the school year runs from September.

Public schools are run by the Ministry of Education, many in partnership with churches, and there are private schools, including church schools and international schools, at both primary and secondary level.

To enrol a child, contact the Ministry of Education or the school directly. You will typically need the child's birth certificate, passport, immunisation record and reports from their previous school. Bring originals and copies, and ask your child's current school abroad for a full transcript and a letter describing the level they have reached, which helps the new school place them in the right class.

Timing is the main challenge for families returning mid-year. Places at popular schools fill quickly, and entry to secondary school is normally organised around the end-of-primary assessment, so a child arriving at secondary age should be discussed with the Ministry well before you move. If your child has special educational needs, raise this early, as support varies between schools.

Children who have studied a different curriculum abroad usually settle well academically, but expect an adjustment to uniforms, longer travel times and, in some subjects, a different syllabus. Homeschooling is allowed but regulated by the Ministry, and some families use online schools for a transition year.

sources.title: The education system in Grenada (Expat Exchange)

title: Working or starting a business
summary: Finding work, registering for tax and National Insurance, and starting a business when you come home.
body:
As a Grenadian national, you do not need a work permit to work in Grenada. A spouse or partner who is not a citizen generally does, so look into their position with the Ministry of Labour before you move rather than after.

Whether you take a job or work for yourself, register with the Inland Revenue Division for a Taxpayer Identification Number, through the G-TAX portal or at the office on the Carenage, and with the National Insurance Scheme. If you were an NIS contributor before you left, take your old NIS number with you. If you have paid social security in another CARICOM country or in Canada, ask the NIS about the reciprocal agreements Grenada has with them, which can allow contributions abroad to count towards a pension.

Many returning nationals bring skills, savings and experience that make self-employment attractive. Our Start a business guide covers choosing a structure, registering with CAIPO, tax and NIS, licences, finance and incentives. The Ministry of Finance has listed tax incentives for returning nationals who set up a business among the benefits of the Welcome Home Programme, so ask the Returning Nationals Facilitation Bureau what is currently available before you import equipment.

If you are looking for employment, local recruitment relies heavily on personal networks, so let people know you are back. Professional qualifications from abroad are generally respected, but regulated professions, such as medicine, nursing, law and engineering, need registration with the relevant council or body before you can practise. Contact them while you are still overseas, as the paperwork can take time.

Finally, list your services or business on Island Connect once you are set up. It is free, and it is how people across both countries find local tradespeople and professionals.

sources.title: Changes to the Returning Nationals Programme, including business incentives (Ministry of Finance)
National Insurance Scheme Grenada: reciprocal agreements
G-TAX: Inland Revenue Division online services

title: Government services
summary: Driving licences, tax and NIS numbers, documents and where to get them in Grenada.
body:
Coming home means re-establishing yourself on several official registers. None is difficult, but each has its own office and paperwork, so it helps to know the order.

Your Taxpayer Identification Number comes from the Inland Revenue Division and is needed for almost everything else, from bank accounts to licences. Register online through the G-TAX portal at tax.gov.gd or in person at the IRD office on the Carenage. Register with the National Insurance Scheme if you will work or be self-employed; you can manage your contributions online at my.nisgrenada.org.

You can drive in Grenada on a valid foreign licence for a limited period after arriving, after which you need a Grenadian driver's licence. Licences have been issued through the Traffic Department of the Royal Grenada Police Force on the Carenage, with the application typically requiring your existing licence, identification and a fee. In 2024 the government announced that vehicle licensing and inspection would move away from the police, so check where to apply when you arrive.

Grenadian passports are issued by the Immigration and Passport Department. If your passport is due to expire within a year or so of your return, renew it before you leave your current country, where a consulate may be able to help, or as soon as you arrive. Birth, marriage and death certificates come from the Registry, and you will need certified copies for school enrolment, property transactions and claims for concessions.

For duty concessions on your household goods and vehicle, the Returning Nationals Facilitation Bureau at the Ministry of Finance is your contact, rather than Customs or Immigration. Keep a folder of certified copies of your key documents; you will use them again and again in your first year back.

title: Returning-national programmes
summary: Duty-free concessions for Vincentians returning home: who qualifies and what they cover.
body:
St Vincent and the Grenadines offers returning nationals duty-free concessions through the Customs and Excise Department. They are aimed at Vincentians who have lived abroad for at least ten years and are coming back to make their permanent home in the country.

The concession covers two things. Household and personal effects, new or used, can be brought in free of all taxes, subject to conditions. One motor vehicle per household, but not a truck, can be imported at a quarter of the normal import duty, excise tax and VAT. The goods can be shipped from abroad or bought in St Vincent from a supplier who operates a private tax-free warehouse.

You must show two things. The first is that you lived abroad for at least ten years, using documents such as payslips, school or university records, bank statements, employment records, visas, residence permits or pension letters. The second is that you intend to settle permanently, which you can support with a house purchase contract, a mortgage, a land title, planning permission for a house, or documents showing you are setting up a business or have a job.

Applications are made in writing on the Customs form to the Comptroller of Customs and Excise at Custom House, Upper Bay Street, Kingstown, and you may be invited to an interview. You must apply within one year of returning.

The published conditions date from some years ago, so confirm the current version with Customs or your nearest SVG consulate before you ship. The details for goods and vehicles are in the following articles.

sources.title: Duty Free Concessions for Returning Nationals: General Conditions (SVG Customs and Excise Department)

title: Planning the move
summary: A timeline for moving home to St Vincent and the Grenadines, built around the Customs conditions.
body:
The returning nationals concession gives you a year after your return to apply, which is more generous than many countries, but a move still goes far more smoothly when the paperwork is gathered before you leave.

Start collecting evidence of your ten or more years abroad while it is easy to obtain: payslips, tax returns, tenancy or mortgage papers, bank statements, residence permits, and your children's school records. Customs looks for proof both of your time abroad and of your intention to settle, so if you are buying a house, have a job offer or are setting up a business, keep copies of those documents too. Check that every family member's passport and birth certificate is in order.

Three to six months before you go, decide what to ship. The concession allows one of each type of household item that you would reasonably need, such as one television and one microwave, so sell or give away duplicates rather than paying freight on items that will be taxed. Prepare an itemised packing list with makes, models and serial numbers, which the Customs form asks for. Get quotes from shippers and choose a customs broker in St Vincent.

Arrange a place to stay for your first weeks and keep originals of important documents in your hand luggage.

After you arrive, apply to the Comptroller of Customs for the concession, then work through your registrations: a TIN with the Inland Revenue Department, the National Insurance Services, a bank account, a driving permit and school places. The articles in this guide explain each step.

sources.title: Duty Free Concessions for Returning Nationals: General Conditions (SVG Customs and Excise Department)

title: Shipping and customs
summary: Bringing household goods to St Vincent and the Grenadines free of tax under the returning nationals concession.
body:
Qualifying returning nationals can bring in household and personal effects completely free of all taxes, whether the items are new or used. The goods can be shipped from abroad or bought locally from a supplier operating a private tax-free warehouse in St Vincent.

The concession is meant to help you set up your home, not to stock a shop, and Customs applies that test. Only one set or item of each type of household good that you would reasonably need is covered: one television, one microwave, one DVD player and so on. Additional items of the same kind may be charged at the full rate of duty.

The goods must be for your own use and kept by you. For four years after import, none of them may be sold, traded, bartered, given away or otherwise disposed of without the permission of the Comptroller of Customs, and permission means paying all the normal taxes. Customs treats breaches seriously: the published conditions warn of fines, imprisonment and seizure of the goods, and the same penalties apply to false declarations.

The application form asks for a full list of your household and personal effects with makes, models and serial numbers where available, together with the name of your agent or broker and the entry numbers for your shipment. A customs broker will prepare the entry and handle clearance at the port, so choose one before your goods arrive and agree the fee.

Apply in writing to the Comptroller of Customs and Excise at Custom House, Upper Bay Street, Kingstown, within one year of returning. If you are invited to an interview, take the documents that support your claim.

sources.title: Duty Free Concessions for Returning Nationals: General Conditions (SVG Customs and Excise Department)

title: Bringing a vehicle
summary: The returning nationals vehicle concession in SVG: what you pay, which vehicles qualify and the four-year rule.
body:
Returning nationals who qualify for the Customs concession can import one motor vehicle per household, but not a truck, on reduced terms. Instead of the full charges, you pay 25 per cent of the normal import duty, excise tax and VAT. The Customs Service Charge is payable in full, and if the vehicle is more than four years old, the vehicle surcharge is also payable in full, which makes newer vehicles considerably better value under the scheme.

The vehicle must be owned by you and registered in your name. As with household goods, you can import it yourself or buy one locally from a supplier operating a private tax-free warehouse, and you must apply to the Comptroller of Customs within one year of your return. The application form asks for the make, model, year, colour, type, engine size and the engine and chassis numbers.

The vehicle must be kept for your own use. It cannot be sold, traded, given away or otherwise disposed of for four years without the Comptroller's permission, and permission means paying the taxes that were waived. Selling it without permission risks a fine, prosecution and seizure.

Before you ship, compare the full cost of freight, the Customs Service Charge, any surcharge and your 25 per cent share of the duties with the price of a comparable vehicle bought locally under the same concession. St Vincent and the Grenadines drives on the left, its roads are steep and narrow in places, and parts and servicing are easiest to find for models already common on the island. Those practical points often favour buying locally.

sources.title: Duty Free Concessions for Returning Nationals: General Conditions (SVG Customs and Excise Department)

title: Housing
summary: Renting, buying and building a home when you return to St Vincent and the Grenadines.
body:
Renting for your first few months is a sensible choice even if you intend to buy or build. It lets you get reacquainted with different districts, test the journey to work or school, and look at property without being rushed.

Rentals are found through estate agents, online listings and, often, through family and friends. Before you sign, ask who pays for water and electricity, whether the house has a water tank, and how it has coped in past storms. In areas close to La Soufrière, ask about volcanic hazard zoning too. Insist on a written tenancy agreement covering the rent, the deposit and notice periods.

If you plan to buy, our Property and investment guide sets out the process, the title checks to insist on, and the costs, including stamp duty on the deed of conveyance. Vincentian citizens do not need an Alien Land Holding Licence, and neither does a spouse who is married to a citizen. Customs also accepts a house purchase contract, mortgage agreement, land title or planning permission as evidence that you are settling permanently, which supports your application for the returning nationals concession.

If you are going to build, perhaps on family land, you will need approval from the Physical Planning and Development Board before work starts, and you should make sure the land is properly in your name first. Family land that has passed down without formal transfers is a common source of delay; a lawyer can advise on putting the title in order, which may involve probate or letters of administration.

Setting up utility accounts usually requires identification and, for tenants, a copy of the lease, so keep both to hand in your first weeks.

title: Banking
summary: Opening an account in St Vincent and the Grenadines, the EC dollar and moving money home.
body:
St Vincent and the Grenadines uses the Eastern Caribbean dollar, issued by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank and shared with other members of the currency union. It is pegged to the US dollar at EC$2.70 to US$1.

The main banking options are the commercial banks, including the Bank of St Vincent and the Grenadines on Halifax Street in Kingstown, and the country's credit unions, which play a large part in everyday saving and lending. Many returning nationals use a bank for international transfers and a credit union for savings and future loans; credit unions are also an important source of housing finance.

To open an account, expect to provide your passport, proof of your local address (a utility bill or tenancy agreement), your Taxpayer Identification Number and, often, a reference from your current bank. If you are bringing savings or the proceeds from selling a home abroad, have documents ready that show where the money came from; banks are required to ask. US citizens and green card holders will also be asked for US tax details.

Open an account soon after you arrive, or before you leave if your bank can arrange it, so that you can pay utility deposits, buy a car and receive any pension. For large transfers, compare the exchange rates and fees from your overseas bank, your new local bank and specialist transfer services; on the sum needed for a house, the difference can be considerable.

If you will receive a pension from abroad, confirm with the paying authority that it can be paid to an account in St Vincent, and keep your old account open until the first payments have arrived.

title: Healthcare
summary: Public hospitals and clinics, user fees, private care and health insurance in St Vincent and the Grenadines.
body:
The Ministry of Health runs public health care in St Vincent and the Grenadines through a network of clinics and health centres for primary care, with hospital care centred on the Milton Cato Memorial Hospital in Kingstown, also known as the Kingstown General Hospital. It is the main public provider of secondary care, such as general surgery and internal medicine. There is also a hospital at Georgetown serving the north of the island.

Public services are not free at the point of use: patients pay user fees, although they are well below the true cost of care. There is no national health insurance scheme, though one has been discussed. Private hospitals, clinics and specialists operate alongside the public system, mainly in and around Kingstown, and are usually paid for at the time of treatment.

Private health insurance is available from regional and international insurers. If you are over 50 or have a long-term condition, compare policies before you leave your current country, as cover is easier to arrange before any new diagnosis. Check whether a policy pays for medical evacuation, because some specialist treatment is only available overseas.

Before moving, collect your medical records, a summary letter from your doctor and a supply of regular medication with the prescriptions, as some brands may differ locally. Register with a doctor or your local clinic soon after you arrive.

If you will be living in the Grenadines, find out where the nearest clinic is and how emergencies are transferred to St Vincent, as services on the smaller islands are more limited.

sources.title: Healthcare in St Vincent and the Grenadines (Pacific Prime)
Milton Cato Memorial Hospital: user fees and national health insurance (Business View Caribbean)

title: Schools
summary: Registering children in St Vincent and the Grenadines' schools, online or in person.
body:
St Vincent and the Grenadines has public, government-assisted and private schools, with education governed by the Education Act. Primary school is followed by secondary school, ending with the Caribbean Secondary Education Certificate examinations, and the school year starts in September.

Registration for children entering kindergarten and early childhood centres in government primary schools normally takes place in May, both online through the Ministry of Education's website, education.gov.vc, and in person at the schools. You will need the child's original birth certificate and immunisation card, and online registration asks you to upload both, including the front and back of the immunisation card.

Families returning from abroad with older children, or arriving mid-year, should contact the Ministry of Education directly to arrange placement. Bring the child's birth certificate, passport, immunisation record and recent school reports, and ask their current school for a transcript and a letter describing the level they have reached.

There is good news on costs. In July 2026 the government announced that registration, processing and admission fees for first-form students entering public and government-assisted secondary schools would be removed, with each school issuing revised registration packages. Ask the school what, if anything, you will still be expected to pay for uniforms, books and activities.

If your child has special educational needs, raise them with the Ministry early, as the Education Act provides for special education programmes but provision varies between schools.

title: Working or starting a business
summary: Tax, National Insurance and setting up on your own when you return to St Vincent and the Grenadines.
body:
Vincentian citizens can work in St Vincent and the Grenadines without a work permit, but a spouse or partner who is not a citizen may need one, so check their position before you move.

Whether employed or self-employed, register with the Inland Revenue Department for a Taxpayer Identification Number, and separately with the National Insurance Services; registering with one does not register you with the other. If you contributed to the NIS before you left, bring your old number. Ask the NIS too about social security agreements that may let contributions made abroad count towards your benefits.

National Insurance rates have risen under reforms that began in 2024. From 1 January 2026, employees pay 6.5 per cent of insurable earnings and employers 7.5 per cent; self-employed contributors pay 13.5 per cent. For someone returning to work for themselves, keeping up NIS contributions is the route to a pension and other benefits, and good standing with the NIS is a condition of some government incentives.

If you plan to start a business, our Start a business guide covers registration with the Commerce and Intellectual Property Office, tax, licences, finance and incentives. Evidence that you are setting up a business also supports your application for the returning nationals concession on your household goods and vehicle.

Regulated professions, such as medicine, nursing, law and engineering, require registration with the relevant council before you can practise, so contact them while you are still abroad. And once you are up and running, list your business or services on Island Connect; it is free.

title: Government services
summary: Driving permits, tax and NIS registration, and dealing with Customs when you return to SVG.
body:
Several government offices will become familiar in your first months home, and knowing which does what saves wasted trips.

The Inland Revenue Department, on Halifax Street in Kingstown, issues your Taxpayer Identification Number and handles income tax and VAT through its e-Tax platform. It is also the licensing authority for driving permits, and Vincentian driving permits carry the holder's TIN.

On driving, the rules depend on where your licence comes from. A valid driving permit issued in another Commonwealth Caribbean country exempts you from needing a Vincentian one. Holders of an international driving permit from a country that has signed the international convention are also exempt, but must register the permit with the Licensing Authority before driving. Visitors with a valid licence from their own country can obtain a temporary permit for up to six months for a fee of EC$125. As a returning resident, plan to obtain a full Vincentian driving permit through the Licensing Authority once you are settled.

The National Insurance Services, separate from the IRD, handles contributions and benefits; register as soon as you start work. For your household goods and vehicle concession, deal with the Comptroller of Customs and Excise at Custom House, Upper Bay Street, Kingstown.

Keep certified copies of your passport, birth certificate, marriage certificate and evidence of your years abroad in one folder. You will need them for Customs, banks, schools and licensing in your first year back.

title: Choosing a structure
summary: Sole trader, partnership or company: what each means in Grenada and when each one makes sense.
body:
Most new businesses in Grenada start as sole traders, and for good reason. It is the cheapest and quickest way to trade legally. If you work under a name other than your own, such as "Island Fresh Juices" rather than "Marcia Joseph", the Registration of Business Names Act requires you to register that name with the Corporate Affairs and Intellectual Property Office (CAIPO). Legally, though, you and the business are the same person. You keep the profits and pay income tax on them personally, and if the business runs up debts you cannot pay, creditors can pursue your own savings and property. The business cannot own land or sign a contract in its own name.

A partnership works the same way for two or more people trading together, and is registered at CAIPO in much the same manner. Each partner is usually liable for the debts of the whole business, which is why a written partnership agreement, prepared or at least reviewed by a lawyer, matters more than most people expect. It should cover who puts in what money, how profits are shared and what happens if one partner wants to leave.

A company, incorporated under the Companies Act, is a separate legal person. It can own property, borrow, employ staff and sign contracts in its own name, and the shareholders' risk is generally limited to what they put in. In return there is more paperwork: a registered office, statutory registers, annual filings with CAIPO and corporation tax returns with the Inland Revenue Division. A company starts to make sense when you are taking on real financial risk, bringing in investors, borrowing seriously from a bank or bidding for contracts with larger clients who prefer to deal with a company.

There is no penalty for starting small and incorporating later, and many businesses do exactly that once they have proved the idea. If you are unsure, an hour with an accountant or lawyer before you register usually costs far less than unpicking the wrong structure afterwards.

sources.title: Grenada Corporate Registry Act and the Acts it administers (Parliament of Grenada)
Grenada Investment Development Corporation: business development services

title: Registering
summary: How to register a business name or incorporate a company at CAIPO, and the registrations that follow.
body:
Registration happens at the Corporate Affairs and Intellectual Property Office (CAIPO) in St George's, which keeps the official registers of business names and companies under the Grenada Corporate Registry Act. Filings can be made at the office or through CAIPO's online services.

The first step for any business is a name search. You give CAIPO one or more proposed names, and it confirms whether they are available. You can then reserve the approved name so that nobody else registers it while you prepare your papers. The fees for searching and reserving are small, but they change from time to time, so check the current figures with CAIPO when you apply.

For a sole trader or partnership, you then register the business name. The application records who you are, the business name, what the business does, where it operates, who owns it and the date it started trading. Once accepted, you receive a certificate of registration, which banks, the Inland Revenue Division and many suppliers will ask to see.

For a company, you file Articles of Incorporation together with notices of the registered office and the directors. The Articles must describe the nature of the business. When everything is in order, CAIPO issues a Certificate of Incorporation and the company legally exists from that date. Most people use a lawyer for this step, particularly if there will be several shareholders.

Registration at CAIPO is not the end. Every business must also register with the Inland Revenue Division for a Taxpayer Identification Number, which can be done online through the G-TAX portal or at the IRD office on the Carenage, and with the National Insurance Scheme. The Grenada Investment Development Corporation (GIDC) offers help with business and company registration and with preparing a business plan, which is worth using if this is your first business.

title: Tax and social security
summary: Registering with the Inland Revenue Division, when VAT applies, and National Insurance for you and your staff.
body:
The Inland Revenue Division (IRD) has been clear that every business in Grenada must be registered with it for tax purposes, whatever its size. Under the Tax Administration Act of 2016, failing to register carries a penalty of $2,500. Registration gives you a Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN), which you will need for licences, bank accounts and government contracts. Since January 2024 the IRD has run its services through G-TAX, an online portal at tax.gov.gd, where you can register, file returns and request tax clearance.

Value Added Tax applies once a business's taxable supplies pass EC$300,000 in a twelve-month period, or are reasonably expected to. VAT-registered businesses charge VAT at the standard rate of 15 per cent, claim back the VAT they pay on business purchases, file regular returns, and must display their VAT registration certificate where customers can see it. Smaller businesses can sometimes register voluntarily if the IRD agrees. Because thresholds and rates are set by law and do change, confirm the current figures with the IRD before you rely on them.

If you employ staff, you must deduct PAYE income tax from their pay and pass it to the IRD each month. You must also register as an employer with the National Insurance Scheme (NIS) and pay contributions on their earnings. The combined rate was 13 per cent in 2025, split between employer and employee, and published guidance for 2026 puts it at 14 per cent, with 7.5 per cent paid by the employer and 6.5 per cent deducted from the employee. Contributions are due within fourteen days of the end of each month, and late payment attracts a 10 per cent surcharge plus monthly interest.

Self-employed people must register with the NIS and pay contributions themselves. The NIS currently gives the self-employed rate as 13.5 per cent of gross earnings, and contributing in one year is what qualifies you for benefits in the next. Payments and records can be managed online through my.nisgrenada.org.

title: Licences
summary: Which businesses need a licence in Grenada, from tourism and taxis to food and alcohol.
body:
Which licences you need depends entirely on what your business does, so it is worth checking before you spend money on premises or equipment.

Tourism businesses are licensed by the Grenada Tourism Authority (GTA) under the Grenada Tourism Authority Act, No. 42 of 2013. That covers taxi drivers, tour operators, tourism attractions, watersports operators, car rental operators, tourist guides and accommodation, from hotels and guest houses to villas, apartments and cottages. Licences are renewed every year through the GTA's Quality Assurance Department, and the GTA only promotes licensed businesses. Car rental operators also need a Taxpayer Identification Number from the Inland Revenue Division before their licence can be approved. If you plan to drive or run tours through Island Connect, your GTA licence is one of the documents we will ask to see.

Anyone handling food for sale, whether cooking, serving, packing or tending bar, needs a food handler's certificate from the Ministry of Health. Premises where food is prepared or sold are also subject to environmental health inspection, so speak to the Ministry's environmental health officers before fitting out a kitchen.

Selling alcohol requires a liquor dealer's licence under the Liquor Dealers' Licences Act. Applications are heard at quarterly licensing sessions held for each parish, and the dates are announced in the Government Gazette.

Vehicles used for hire, haulage or rental must carry the right registration and pass inspection. In 2024 the government announced that vehicle licensing and inspection would move away from the Royal Grenada Police Force, so confirm the current office and procedure before you buy or import a vehicle for business use.

Regulated professions and financial services, such as pharmacies, banking, insurance and money transfer, each have their own regulator and licensing rules. A short conversation with the relevant ministry or authority at the planning stage can save a great deal of time later.

title: Finance
summary: Where small businesses in Grenada find money to start or grow, and what lenders will ask for.
body:
Most small businesses in Grenada are started with the owner's own savings, help from family, or a modest loan, and it pays to know what each source of finance expects before you ask.

Commercial banks, including Republic Bank Grenada and the Grenada Co-operative Bank, offer business accounts, overdrafts and loans. Credit unions are often more willing to lend to new and small businesses, particularly to members with a savings history, and their terms can be more flexible. The Grenada Development Bank exists to finance development and small enterprise, and is worth approaching for projects that commercial banks consider too small or too new.

Whoever you approach, expect to be asked for the same things: a clear business plan with realistic figures, your CAIPO registration certificate, your Taxpayer Identification Number and evidence that your tax and National Insurance affairs are up to date, details of any security you can offer, and records of income if you are already trading. Lenders are far more comfortable with a business that keeps proper books from the start, even simple ones.

The Grenada Investment Development Corporation (GIDC) runs a business development service for small and medium-sized enterprises. It helps with business plans and offers training in financial management, bookkeeping, customer service, customs procedures and digital business. A business plan prepared with the GIDC's help tends to be taken more seriously by lenders.

Grant programmes for small businesses appear from time to time, often funded by regional or international partners, and usually run for a fixed period. Ask the GIDC what is open when you are ready to apply, and be wary of anyone who charges a fee to "guarantee" a grant.

title: Incentives
summary: How Grenada's investment incentives work, which sectors they favour and how to apply through the GIDC.
body:
Grenada's investment incentives are handled by the Grenada Investment Development Corporation (GIDC), the government's investment promotion agency. Rather than a fixed menu of benefits, Grenada operates a performance-based regime: each proposal is assessed on its likely contribution to the economy, and larger investments with more jobs, exports or local spending attract more support.

The incentives available can include relief from customs duties on equipment and materials brought in for an approved project, investment allowances and tax credits. The GIDC gives priority to tourism, agribusiness, health and wellness, information and communications technology, renewable energy and the creative industries, though projects in other sectors can still apply.

The practical route is to contact the GIDC with a written proposal that sets out what you plan to do, how much you will invest, how many people you expect to employ and what you will need to import. The GIDC evaluates it and advises on what you may qualify for. Concessions must be approved before you import or buy, because relief is not normally granted retrospectively on goods that have already cleared customs.

For smaller businesses, the most valuable support is often the GIDC's business development service rather than tax relief: help with business plans and registration, and training in bookkeeping, customs procedures and digital business. If you are just starting out, begin there and ask whether any incentive applies to your plans.

title: Choosing a structure
summary: Sole proprietor, partnership or company: what each means in St Vincent and the Grenadines.
body:
In St Vincent and the Grenadines, the simplest way to start is as a sole proprietor, registering your business name with the Commerce and Intellectual Property Office (CIPO) in Kingstown. You and the business are legally the same person: profits are taxed as your personal income, and you are personally responsible for the business's debts. It suits most one-person trades and services, and it is quick and inexpensive to set up.

A partnership is the same arrangement for two or more people, and each partner is generally liable for the debts of the whole business. Put the terms in writing before you start, covering money put in, how profits are shared and what happens if someone leaves, and have a lawyer review it.

A domestic company, incorporated under the Companies Act, is a separate legal person that can own property, borrow and contract in its own name, with shareholders' risk generally limited to their investment. It brings more administration, including a registered office, annual filings and corporation tax returns to the Inland Revenue Department. Since 1 January 2023 the corporation tax rate and the top rate of personal income tax have both been 28 per cent, so the choice is rarely about tax rates alone. It is more often about limiting personal risk, bringing in investors or meeting the expectations of larger customers.

Overseas companies that want to trade locally register as external companies. Business Companies formed through the Financial Services Authority are designed for international business and are not the right vehicle for trading on St Vincent or in the Grenadines.

Starting as a sole proprietor and incorporating later is common and perfectly sensible. Take advice from an accountant or lawyer if you expect to borrow heavily, employ several people or take on investors.

title: Registering
summary: Registering a business name or company with CIPO in Kingstown, then with the IRD and NIS.
body:
Businesses in St Vincent and the Grenadines are registered with the Commerce and Intellectual Property Office (CIPO), on the first floor of Brewster's Building, McCoy Street, Kingstown. The office can be reached on +1 784 456 1516, and its forms are published on cipo.gov.vc.

A sole proprietor or partnership completes the Application for Registration of a Business, giving the business name, the owners, the nature of the business and where it operates. CIPO also publishes the forms you will need later: one for changing the registered particulars, such as a new address or partner, and a Notice of Cessation for when a business closes. Keeping these up to date matters, because the register is what banks and government departments check.

A company starts with approval of its proposed name, followed by the incorporation documents and notices of its registered office and directors. CIPO publishes a list of lawyers and local agents, and most people use one for incorporation, particularly when there are several shareholders.

Registering with CIPO does not register you for tax or social security. Each business must separately register with the Inland Revenue Department (IRD) on Halifax Street, Kingstown, which issues a Taxpayer Identification Number for the taxes that apply to you, and with the National Insurance Services (NIS). The IRD's online services are available through its e-Tax platform.

If you would like help with a business plan before you register, the Centre for Enterprise Development (CED) offers business counselling and plan preparation, and Invest SVG can advise on larger or export-focused projects.

title: Tax and social security
summary: Income tax, VAT and National Insurance in St Vincent and the Grenadines, including the 2026 NIS rates.
body:
Every business needs a Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN) from the Inland Revenue Department (IRD), which also administers income tax, PAYE and Value Added Tax. Returns and payments can be made through the IRD's e-Tax platform.

Since 1 January 2023, the corporation tax rate and the top rate of personal income tax have been 28 per cent, reduced from 30 per cent, and the standard personal deduction rose from $20,000 to $22,000. Sole proprietors pay personal income tax on their business profits; companies pay corporation tax on theirs.

A business must register for VAT once its taxable sales reach EC$300,000 in a twelve-month period. The standard rate is 16 per cent, with a reduced rate of 11 per cent for hotel accommodation. VAT-registered businesses charge VAT on their sales, reclaim the VAT on their business purchases and file monthly returns. Thresholds and rates are set by law and do change, so confirm them with the IRD before you rely on them.

National Insurance is a separate registration with the National Insurance Services (NIS), and registering with the IRD does not register you with the NIS. Contribution rates have been rising under a reform programme that began in 2024. From 1 January 2026 the rate for employees is 14 per cent of insurable earnings, of which the employer pays 7.5 per cent and the employee 6.5 per cent. Self-employed contributors pay 13.5 per cent and voluntary contributors 12.84 per cent.

Employers deduct PAYE and the employee's NIS share from wages and pay both, together with the employer's NIS share, each month. Self-employed people, including drivers and tradespeople working for themselves, are strongly encouraged to contribute: it is the only route to an NIS pension and other benefits, and good standing with the NIS is a condition of some government incentives.
